items.title: William Russell Interview, 1975-02-02
items.q: Gene Williams had heard these records and agreed with me too that at least Bunk showed some possibilities... Gene's idea was more or less to try to preserve Bunk's tone and Bunk's playing as much as we could get.

ctx.x: Well, you could tell me how American music got started. It started at the beginning.

So anyway, to get back to the point, Gene Williams had heard these records and agreed with me too that at least Bunk showed some possibilities. You couldn't really tell much how he played, both because his lip wasn't in shape and just by himself. The type of trumpet playing that Bunk did, which was a remarkable thing, and yet by itself it wouldn't sound that effective. Bunk was hardly ever on the beat, so if you didn't hear him patting his foot and all there, you could really tell of course where the beat is, but…

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1975-02-02
items.q: Louie and Bunks and those people got.

ctx.x: Well, of course, we'll never know what Joe Oliver really sounded like.

No, that's right. On the records, you can't tell how big his tone was. But from all the evidence, about 100% of it, you might say, of anybody that ever talked about him in the old days that heard him, talk about the big tone. That he was almost like, say, a second Bolden after Bolden, that he had that big tone. Which would have undoubtedly been bigger than Louie. However, Joe did use a lot of these freak effects, not only hats and maybe plungers and all—not so much plungers. He had this little con mute, a little…
What about— Well, anyway, I guess if there's anything else to talk about.
